title: Upgrading to TLS Within HTTP/1.1
summary: Explains how to use the HTTP/1.1 Upgrade mechanism to start Transport Layer Security (TLS) over an existing TCP connection. This lets a server offer secure and plain HTTP on the same connection endpoint. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: You start talking to someone normally, then both agree to switch to a secret code partway through, without hanging up and calling again.

questions: how to upgrade http to tls
what is the http connect method
what is the upgrade header in http
subtitle: How HTTP/1.1 can switch an open connection to TLS, plus the CONNECT method for tunnels through proxies.

tldr.problem: Secure web traffic needed its own port (443) and URI scheme, which halves the number of well-known ports and makes name-based virtual hosting with TLS hard.
tldr.mechanism: Client or server uses the HTTP/1.1 Upgrade header with the token TLS/1.0 to switch an existing connection on port 80 to TLS. A 426 Upgrade Required status signals a mandatory upgrade, and CONNECT sets up end-to-end tunnels through proxies.
tldr.outcome: The RFC updates RFC 2616 and does not change how https: URIs work. It is itself updated by RFC 7230 and RFC 7231.

today: RFC 2817 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2616 and has itself been updated by RFC 7230 and RFC 7231. The text states that it does not change the definition of the https URI scheme.

sections.title: Why Upgrade Instead of a Second Port
sections.content:
Historically HTTP over SSL was told apart from plain HTTP by a unique URI scheme and TCP port: http on port 80, https on port 443. Other protocols asked for parallel ports too, which effectively halves the number of available well-known ports. In December 1997 the Applications Area Directors and the IESG reaffirmed that issuing parallel "secure" ports should be deprecated.

The RFC notes there was little interest in alternatives to port 443 for generic web browsing, and nothing in it changes how https: URIs are interpreted. New protocols built on HTTP, such as the Internet Printing Protocol, wanted the upgrade mechanism.

The mechanism also helps virtual hosting. The TLS handshake did not name the intended host, relying on the IP address alone. A cleartext Upgrade request first lets the server pick a certificate using the Host: header, enabling secure name-based virtual hosting.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of building a whole second front door just for secret conversations, you use the same door and then switch to whispering once inside.

sections.title: Client Requested Upgrade
sections.content:
A client sends an HTTP/1.1 request with Upgrade: TLS/1.0 (and, as HTTP/1.1 requires, Connection: Upgrade) to ask the server to finish the current request after switching to TLS/1.0.

In an optional upgrade, the client offers the switch on any clear request where an unsecured answer would be acceptable. The server MAY answer normally or switch. If an unsecured response would be unacceptable, the client MUST first send an OPTIONS * request to complete the switch.

If the server is ready to start the handshake, it MUST send 101 Switching Protocols with an Upgrade header listing the protocol stack bottom-up, for example TLS/1.0, HTTP/1.1. Once the handshake succeeds, the server MUST continue with the response to the original request. Any handshake failure MUST lead to disconnection.
sections.plainLanguage: The client says "can we switch to secret code?" The server says "yes, switching now," they swap codes, and then the server answers the original question.

sections.title: Server Requested Upgrade
sections.content:
A server can advertise upgrades with the Upgrade response header. In any response other than 101 or 426 it MAY list protocols it is willing to switch to.

To insist, the server MAY use the new status code 426 Upgrade Required, which MUST include an Upgrade header naming the required TLS version. The server SHOULD add a human-readable message body explaining the reason and any alternatives.

A client willing to use TLS cannot start the handshake right after the 426. It must use the client-requested operations described above to proceed.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the server is the one who says "I only talk in secret code." The client then has to ask to switch properly before the server will answer.

sections.title: Upgrade Across Proxies and CONNECT
sections.content:
Upgrade is a hop-by-hop header, so a request with it sent to a proxy asks to change the protocol between the client and the proxy only. TLS needs end-to-end connectivity for authentication and to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks, so the RFC documents the CONNECT method to build a tunnel through proxies first. Afterwards any of the normal upgrade operations can run.

The CONNECT request-target is always an authority, a host name and port separated by a colon, such as server.example.com:80. Other HTTP mechanisms, such as proxy authentication, can be used with it. Any 2xx response means the proxy has connected to the host and port and is now tunneling. A proxy MUST NOT send a 2xx unless it has a direct or tunnel connection to the authority, and it SHOULD itself use CONNECT when it must go through a further proxy.

A proxy that does not recognize 426 might strip the accompanying Upgrade header. A client that receives a 426 without it needs to request an end-to-end tunnel and repeat the request.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper in the middle, called a proxy, would only switch codes with you, not with the final server. So you first ask the helper to dig a private tunnel to the server, and talk secretly through it.

sections.title: Why a 4xx Status Code
sections.content:
The RFC explains why 426 is a client-error code and not a redirect. A 3xx code for "Upgrade Required" would be treated by an unaware user agent as plain 300. It would look for a Location header and retry at that URL, and since it still would not know to upgrade to TLS, it would at best fail again.

A 4xx code gives an unambiguous failure signal and lets the server say exactly which protocol extensions a resource must be served with.
sections.plainLanguage: If the server just pointed the client to a different address, a client that does not know about secret codes would go there and still fail. Saying "you made a mistake, here is what is needed" is clearer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker could delete the Upgrade header, which is the same risk as rewriting pages to change https:// links to http://. The risk exists only if the server offers the same information over secure and insecure channels. A client that knows a server supports TLS can insist by sending an Upgrade request with a no-op method like OPTIONS. Users should still examine the certificate the server presents.

Widespread use of this mechanism could mean http identifies both secure and non-secure resources. The security required is left to client and server to decide.

A generic TCP tunnel is risky. CONNECT authorization should be limited to a small number of known ports, and the Upgrade mechanism here only needs onward tunneling at port 80. Tunneled data is opaque to the proxy, so a client connecting to port 25 could, for example, relay spam over SMTP.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky person in the middle could hide the "want to switch?" message. And a tunnel is like a private passage, so a proxy should only dig it to a few safe places.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
The RFC asks IANA to create two registries: HTTP Status Codes and HTTP Upgrade Tokens. The status code registry starts with the values from HTTP/1.1, WebDAV (420 to 424), WebDAV Advanced Collections (425) and this memo (426). New values SHOULD go through a standards track review in the IETF Applications Area.

Upgrade tokens follow the form token ["/" product-version] and are registered First Come First Served. Rules include that a registered token stays registered forever and that each registration MUST name a responsible party and a point of contact. This memo defines the token TLS/1.0.
sections.plainLanguage: There are official lists of status numbers and upgrade names, so everyone uses the same words for the same things.
